query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of aluminum to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the in situ formation of an adherent aluminum oxide (Al2O3) scale at high temperatures, thereby enhancing its oxygen resistance in air while preserving its desirable mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition of aluminum (approximately 3 atomic %) into the cast HfNbTaTiZr composition.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at approximately 800 °C for 5 hours, with expected strain rates similar to previous mechanical tests (10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(–1)) and preservation of cast microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 surface layer that acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum atoms preferentially oxidize to form a protective Al2O3 film. This layer impedes further oxygen ingress ('pesting') without significantly altering the bulk phase or the mechanical properties of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit markedly improved oxidation resistance (i.e., reduced pesting and oxidation-related degradation) after 5 h exposure at 800 °C, while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength as the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows inadequate oxygen resistance under high-temperature air exposure despite its acceptable mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under high-temperature (approximately 800 °C) air exposure for durations of up to 5 hours in cast-state specimens. It is assumed that the modest Al addition will not significantly alter the original phase composition or compromise the alloy's mechanical properties under the test conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum content and the long-term stability of the alumina scale under cyclic or longer exposures require further investigation. There is also uncertainty regarding any potential subtle interactions of Al with the high-entropy alloy matrix that might affect mechanical performance in unforeseen ways.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one set with approximately 3 at% aluminum addition and one set as the control. Subject both sets to an air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours. Following exposure, examine the surface oxide layers using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) combined with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to assess the presence and adherence of Al2O3. Additionally, perform tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature to compare ductility and yield strength between the two sets.
measurements: Characterization of oxide scale thickness, continuity, and composition (via SEM/EDS).
Room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength measurements.
Weight gain measurements for oxidation rate assessment.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the Al-doped alloy does not form a protective, adherent alumina scale (i.e., exhibiting similar or increased oxidation and pesting compared to the control) or if the alloy’s mechanical properties (ductility and high-temperature strength) deteriorate significantly relative to the untreated material.

Snoek-type damping performance in strong and ductile high-entropy alloys

Abstract: We developed high-temperature high-damping high-entropy alloys with superior mechanical properties via Snoek relaxation. Noise and mechanical vibrations not only cause damage to devices, but also present major public health hazards. High-damping alloys that eliminate noise and mechanical vibrations are therefore required. Yet, low operating temperatures and insufficient strength/ductility ratios in currently available high-damping alloys limit their applicability. Using the concept of high-entropy alloy (HEA), we present a class of high-damping materials. The design is based on refractory HEAs, solid-solutions doped with either 2.0 atomic % oxygen or nitrogen, (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98O2 and (Ta0.5Nb0.5HfZrTi)98N2. The model HEAs also exhibit a high tensile yield strength of ~1400 MPa combined with a large ductility of ~20%. Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System

Abstract: Refractory high entropy alloys (HEA) are promising materials for high temperature applications. This work presents investigations of the room temperature tensile mechanical properties of selected 3 and 4 elements medium entropy alloys (MEA) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system. Tensile testing was combined with fractographic and microstructure analysis, using scanning electron microscope (SEM), wavelength dispersive spectroscope (WDS) and X-Ray powder diffraction (XRD). The 5 element HEA alloy HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and elongation while 4 and 3 element MEAs have lower strength. Some of them are ductile, some of them brittle, depending on microstructure. Simultaneous presence of Ta and Zr in the alloy resulted in a significant reduction of ductility caused by reduction of the BCC phase content. Precipitation of Ta rich particles on grain boundaries reduces further the maximum elongation to failure down to zero values.
